young.html: Dante Alighieri was a poet in the city of Florence, in Italy, about 700 years ago. He wrote a giant poem about an imaginary journey through the three realms where, as Christians of his time believed, souls go after death: Hell, Purgatory and Heaven. The first part, the Inferno, is the journey through Hell.

The poem begins with Dante lost in a dark forest at night. He tries to climb a sunny hill, but three wild animals block his path: a spotted leopard, a lion and a hungry wolf. Just when he is ready to give up, a figure appears. It is the spirit of Virgil, a Roman poet Dante loved, who has come to guide him. The only way out, Virgil says, is the long way: down through the whole of Hell, and up the other side.

young.name: gb-dante-cosmos
young.cap: Hell is shaped like a giant funnel with nine circles, each smaller than the one above. Step down through them with the buttons, or tap a circle.

young.html: Each circle is for a different kind of wrong, and the worst wrongs are at the bottom. Things in Hell happen in ways that fit the wrong: people who let their feelings blow them about are blown by a never-ending wind. At the very bottom is a lake of ice, and in the middle of it, stuck fast, is Satan. Dante and Virgil climb right past him, and at last they come out on the other side of the world, under the stars.
For parents: the Inferno has frightening scenes. Young readers can enjoy Cantos I to IV (the dark wood, the gate and Limbo), and the climb out at the end of Canto XXXIV, or a good retelling.

A rhyme chain. Dante wrote in three-line groups where the middle line's rhyme starts the next group: A B A, B C B, C D C. Try it: "The night was long, the forest deep, / I saw no path, I saw no light, / until a voice called through my sleep." Now the next group must rhyme with light in lines 1 and 3. Can you write two more?

young.name: gb-terza-rima
young.cap: Add tercets and watch the rhymes chain together.

full.html: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) was born in Florence. As a boy he met Beatrice Portinari, who became, in his writing, the great love and guide of his life; she died young in 1290, and he wrote of her in La Vita Nuova ("The New Life"). He served Florence in its fierce political quarrels, and in 1302, while he was away, the winning party sentenced him to exile. He never returned. He wrote the Comedy in exile, finishing it shortly before his death in Ravenna.

He called it simply the Comedy, because it begins in sorrow and ends in joy, and because it is written in the everyday language of Tuscany rather than in Latin. Later readers added "Divine." It has three parts, or canticles, Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso, of 34, 33 and 33 cantos: 100 in all. The journey takes place at Easter in the year 1300, when Dante was 35, "midway" through the Bible's span of seventy years.

full.text:
In the midway of this our mortal life,
I found me in a gloomy wood, astray
Gone from the path direct ...
full.author: Dante
full.note: Cary turned Dante's rhymed verse into unrhymed blank verse.

full.html: Dante wrote in terza rima, a rhyme pattern he invented: three-line stanzas rhyming ABA BCB CDC, each one linked to the next. A canto ends with a single line that closes the last rhyme. In Italian the first three lines end vita, oscura, smarrita.

full.cap: Count the lines: n tercets plus one closing line make 3n + 1.

full.title: Counting lines
full.q: A canto has 46 tercets, plus its closing line. How many lines is that?
full.a: 139 lines (Inferno, Canto I, has 136; cantos range from about 115 to 160)

full.html: Virgil explains that he was sent by Beatrice, from Heaven, to rescue Dante. Dante chose Virgil because Virgil's Aeneid had already taken a hero into the underworld, and because Virgil was his master in poetry. In the poem Virgil stands for the best that human reason can do, guiding Dante as far as reason can go.

full.text:
Through me the way is to the city dolent;
Through me the way is to eternal dole;
Through me the way among the people lost.
Justice incited my sublime Creator;
Created me divine Omnipotence,
The highest Wisdom and the primal Love.
Before me there were no created things,
Only eterne, and I eternal last.
All hope abandon, ye who enter in!
full.work: Inferno, Canto III (the words over the gate of Hell)
full.author: Dante

full.name: gb-dante-cosmos
full.cap: The nine circles from the gate to the center of the Earth, with our own short summaries.

full.html: In Canto XI Virgil explains the plan, using Aristotle's Ethics. The upper circles (2 to 5) hold sins of incontinence, failing to control one's desires. Below the walls of the city of Dis lie the sins of malice, done on purpose: first violence (circle 7), then fraud, which is worse because it misuses reason, the gift that makes us human (circles 8 and 9). Treachery against those who trusted you is the very worst.

Each punishment fits its sin, an idea later readers call the contrapasso ("counter-suffering"), from a word one of Dante's characters uses in Canto XXVIII. Those who let desire sweep them along are swept by wind; the angry fight in mud; the cold-hearted traitors are held in ice. The punishments show what the sin was already like.

Dante feels pity for many of the souls he meets. In Canto V, two lovers tell their sad story and he faints from sorrow. Later he grows harder, and Virgil approves. Readers still argue whether the poem wants us to share his pity or to learn to see as divine justice sees.

In the eighth circle, among false advisers, Dante meets the Greek hero Ulysses (Odysseus) wrapped in a flame. Ulysses tells a story found in no ancient book: in old age he sailed his crew west past the edge of the known world, urging them on with a famous speech.

full.text:
"O brothers!" I began, "who to the west
Through perils without number now have reach'd;
To this the short remaining watch, that yet
Our senses have to wake, refuse not proof
Of the unpeopled world, following the track
Of Phoebus. Call to mind from whence ye sprang:
Ye were not form'd to live the life of brutes,
But virtue to pursue and knowledge high."
full.author: Dante

full.html: They sail for five months and see a great mountain rising from the sea, and then a storm sinks them. Ulysses' thirst for knowledge is noble; he is in Hell for the tricks of his war, such as the wooden horse of Troy. Readers take the mountain to be Purgatory, the subject of the next canticle.

At the center of the Earth, in the frozen lake, Satan is stuck in ice, and the beating of his huge wings is what freezes it. Virgil carries Dante down Satan's side; past the center, "down" becomes "up," and the two climb a long passage to the far side of the Earth. The canticle ends as they come out to see the stars. All three canticles end with the same word: stelle, "stars."

Reading the Inferno as a list of horrors. Dante's Hell is a moral map: each circle asks what a wrong does to the person who chooses it. And it is only one third of the journey; the poem's aim is the climb that follows.

deep.html: Medieval readers looked for several senses in a text: the literal story, and beneath it allegorical, moral and spiritual meanings. The Comedy invites this. Literally, it is one man's journey; allegorically, it is every soul's journey from confusion to clarity. A letter to Dante's patron, Cangrande della Scala, explains the poem this way; scholars still debate whether Dante wrote it.

Dante fills his Hell with people his readers knew: politicians, churchmen, even popes, along with figures from myth and history. His harsh judgments of his own city were part of the poem's power and its risk. He presents these as his judgments within the poem; later readers have often disagreed with them.

About fifty years after Dante's death, Florence paid Boccaccio to lecture on the poem in public, and a 1555 edition first printed the title La Divina Commedia. In English, Henry Francis Cary's blank-verse version (1814) made Dante widely read; Longfellow's line-by-line translation (1867) and Charles Eliot Norton's prose (1891) followed. Painters, composers and poets have returned to it ever since.

items: Is it right for a poet to place real people in Hell? What does Dante risk by doing it?
Is fraud worse than violence, as Dante says? Why might misusing reason be the worst wrong?
Why does Dante pity some sinners, and why does Virgil scold him for it?
What does Ulysses get right, and what does he get wrong?

deep.html: Dante built on Virgil's Aeneid (Book VI) and on Aquinas's and Aristotle's accounts of virtue and vice, all earlier on this ladder. Milton's Paradise Lost, later on, offers another great poem of Hell and its fallen angel.

questions: If you were lost in a dark wood, who would you want for a guide, and why?
Dante says each punishment fits its wrong. Is a punishment that "fits" fairer than one that does not?
Dante felt sorry for some of the people he met. Is it good to feel sorry for someone who did wrong?
Ulysses says we were made "virtue to pursue and knowledge high." What do you most want to learn?
Why do you think all three parts of the poem end with the word "stars"?
care: The Inferno describes the punishments of Hell vividly. This lesson summarizes them gently and quotes none of them. Young readers can follow Cantos I to IV and the end of Canto XXXIV, or a retelling.
